description:
Triangulate Comb-foot (Steatoda triangulosa) aka Triangulated Cobweb Spider - female

3 October 2015: We came upon a female Triangulate Comb-foot (Steatoda triangulosa) Spider (aka Triangulated Cobweb Spider) in the vicinity adjoining Avondale Park. We provide six images of this species which is now a global species originally from Eurasia. In this sense it is an invasive or introduced species though no cases of envenomation by this species of humans have been reported. Rather, it is a spider that preys on other spiders and various insects including the Brown Recluse Spider whose venom and bites are known to be adverse to humans. 

Triangulate Comb-foot Spider is a common house spider and is considered harmless to humans.

We thank Dr. Margarethe Brummermann for having responded promptly to our query for its IDentification which was placed on BugGuide. It was her ID that made possible this observation on iNaturalist. To access the BugGuide ID go here: http://bugguide.net/node/view/1149469

Sources:

"Triangulate Cobweb Spider," Wikipedia, description, accessed 10.4.15, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulate_cobweb_spider

"Triangulate Comb-foot (Steatoda triangulosa)," iNaturalist, description and observations made to date per this species, accessed, 10.4.15, http://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/81579-Steatoda-triangulosa

description:
7 part photostory, this one is for the spider which can be seen in 2nd and succeeding photos.
Photo 1: 
I Thought It Was A Yellowjacket 
When I came inside my house, what I thought was a yellow jacket came in with me. This is a problem because I like to go barefoot and I have cats that could get stung also. I went to get a broom to try to slap it down out of the air. When I came back it had gone to a window with blinds. I discovered that a tiny spider had solved my problem. The "yellow jacket" had been caught in a web. Later when I got the insect identified by experts, it turned out to be a fly pretending to be a yellow jacket. This is an example of Batesian mimicry which is when a harmless, tasty species mimics another species that is toxic or foul tasting or dangerous in order to be protected from predators. Sure fooled me. It did not deter the spider. 
Photo 2: 
Spider To The Rescue 
The spider solved my problem. Here is the spider coming to take a look at what it caught in its web. I was shooting these photos through open blinds. 
Photo 3: 
Underside Of The Spider 
I took this shot to help with getting an id on the spider. 
Photo 4: 
Topside Of The Spider 
As the spider wrapped some silk around the fly's legs, I got a shot of the top side of the spider. 
Photo 5: 
Uncropped Shot For Perspective 
I left this shot uncropped to show how I was having to do this, shooting between two blinds slats.

This spider was found under the bark of the Eucalyptus tree where I usually discover them. "The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile."

"The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile."

description: Observed under the bark of a Eucalyptus tree.

This spider was found under the bark of the Eucalyptus tree where I usually discover them. The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile.

"The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile."

Similar to the true black widow, the false black widow female is 6 to 10.5 millimeters in length, but it lacks the red hourglass pattern on the underside of the abdomen, which is more oval in shape than that of the true black widow. In most specimens, the abdomen has a purplish-brown to black color with light, pale-yellow to grayish markings. In many specimens, these markings may be faded and difficult to see. The cephalothorax is a red-brown color with slightly darker legs.

False black widows produce symptoms that are similar to but much less severe than those of a true black widow bite. There are documented cases of Steatoda bites leading to blistering at the site of the bite and a general malaise lasting for several days.

Eight Steatoda species occur in the United States, including S. grossa, which is found along the coastal states of the Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific regions.

description:
I usually observe the Noble False Widow spider in a tubular web retreat that is usually concealed
 under the bark of a Eucalyptus tree. 

"The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile."

"The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile."

description:
A False Black Widow (Steatoda grossa), photographed in the restrooms at New Brighton State Beach in Capitola, CA.  Note the flat-topped abdomen that is dark brown in color, except for the pale pattern on its upper abdominal surface.  The pattern - a pale horseshoe mark at the anterior end of the abdomen, followed by three longitudinal series of small, whitish triangles - is typical for S. grossa.  Adult female Western Black Widows (Latrodectus hesperus) are often confused with S. grossa; however, the abdomens of adult female L. hesperus are always shiny black in color, not brown, with an upper abdominal surface that has no pattern at all (the famous hourglass mark is on the lower abdominal surface). The legs of adult female L. hesperus are also significantly longer than the legs of S. grossa.

The spider in my photograph was fairly large, as spiders go, with a body length measuring ~10mm (from pedipalps to spinnerets).

description:
I usually observe the Noble False Widow spider in a tubular web retreat that is usually concealed
 under the bark of a Eucalyptus tree. 

"The Noble False Widow, Steatoda nobilis (Thorell, 1875) (Araneae, Theridiidae), is, due to its relatively large size and potential medical importance, one of the most notable invasive spider species worldwide. Probably originating from the Canary Islands and Madeira, the species is well established in Western Europe and large parts of the Mediterranean area and has spread recently into California and South America, while Central European populations were not known until 2011.
In the Americas, the populations in California have to be established only recently. Vetter et al. (2015) pointed out that only very recently pictures and records of S. nobilis have been sent to an address originally used for records of Latrodectus geometricus, another alien theridiid which has settled in California. In Chile, records from four cities are currently known. Besides the records from Concepción and Temuco (Taucare-Ríos et al. 2016), observations of S. nobilis in Valdivia and Pucón are mentioned in Ceryngier et al. (2018). Concepción and Valdivia, both cities with large harbour areas, are separated by a distance of over 300 km. These records show that S. nobilis is widespread in Chile."

description:
Once more in my apartment, as I was brushing my teeth I caught sight of a black spider nestled in the corner of my ceiling. My immediate assumption leaned towards it being a black widow given their very common in the Bay Area. The spider showcased a dark brownish abdomen adorned with distinctive yellowish stripes. Notably its legs exhibited a yellowish hint reminiscent of new spring leaves and were notably elongated. Despite the resemblance to a black widow this particular arachnid appeared slightly longer and more skittish in its movements. It had a distinctive marking on its abdomen, resembling a skull, adding an element of uniqueness to its appearance. Observing this spider highlighted the diverse arachnid residents that coexist within the urban spaces we occupy. The subtle variations in coloration and markings underscored the complexity and adaptability of these creatures, each contributing to the intricate tapestry of life within the walls of my apartment.
 11/02/2023 Mathew Oliveira-Killmon

description:
First found this beautiful girl under our front door porch corner.  Thought at first she was a black widow, but after taking a closer look, thought possibly a brown widow, but there was something strange about her with a distinctive mark on her back abdomen.  After doing some research, I found that she was actually a Noble False Widow.  They are distinct by having a pattern that is some looks exactly like a human skull which after looking at some oneline, I became facilitated by their evolution to have this distinctive pattern on their back and how an image of a scary human face or skull came to be!

After I found her, I started looking around the yard as I found out they are invasive and will take over other spiders nests (either abandoned or eats the current spider) as they don’t like to make their own.  Now after going into the yard, I saw at least 8 other females either her size or larger and saw some of them recently had their eggs hatched.  The next evening I went through our yard and our patio which is wood and on the second floor.  I found a small hatchling every years from each other.  I decided to kill the hatchlings and any males found in the yard (only found 2 males of breeding size) and left the large females alone.  Within the span of a month, the entire yard is now covered in webs all around our plants, bushes and small trees.  It looks like most the webs were once orb weavers, but now they have noble false widows in them.  They seem to run away every chance they get, and have never once come inside the house as we leave all of our doors and windows open for the entire day.  All we’ve had is a few grass spiders and one brown house spider that looks similar to a brown recluse, probably escaping from the Noble False Widows.  

We can get rid of them anytime, but so far, even with most of our yard being covered by Widows, they have been more of a benefit than anything and the females will stay put in the same spot unless their nest is disturbed.  But I will end with this, basically they have made their way this far South and I do think anything can stop their progress in becoming the dominant species in this area as they actually have been known to kill other brown/black widows and brown recluses.  The only damage is the variety of indigenous spiders being wiped out, but as long as they stay timid and afraid, I would take them over widows and recluses any day!
